entries.note: There is no shared threshold for becoming a central issue. The reference to his expectations also concerns a private belief.

entries.test: Public technical proofs or a demonstrably jailbreak-proof LLM guardrail would settle whether uncircumventable LLM guardrails are possible.
entries.note: Marcus explicitly endorses the experts' impossibility claim for LLMs. Repeated successful jailbreaks alone cannot prove universal impossibility.

entries.test: Public evaluations of guardrails available by January 2024, measuring both unsafe compliance and refusal of legitimate requests, would test whether any effectively balanced the two.
entries.note: This is an explicitly endorsed quotation of Marcus's own coauthored work. Effectiveness allows some judgment, but the safety-versus-usability tradeoff has a plain empirical reading.

entries.test: Public evaluations of guardrails available by June 17, 2026, measuring unsafe compliance and refusal of legitimate requests, would test whether any effectively balanced the two.
entries.note: “That’s still true” renews the preceding claim at publication.

entries.test: Public descriptions of next-token prediction objectives, architectures, and safety mechanisms would test whether safety is built into their predictive design.
entries.note: The drafter adds an explicit causal explanation for guardrail failure and strengthens the statement with “inherently.” The original asserts a property of the technology's design.
This presents a policy choice about restricting LLMs and tolerating their harms. It supplies no specific outcome to test.

entries.test: Public jailbreak evaluations and security analyses across generative AI systems from multiple developers would test whether the vulnerability extends beyond Anthropic.
entries.note: The general claim concerns a shared technological problem; it need not mean every individual system has an identical vulnerability.
